AltText: Calhau de São Jorge, a beach composed of rounded boulders and stones on Madeira, with steep cliffs in the background.
Title: Shaped by river and sea
Description:
Calhau de São Jorge on Madeira. “Calhau” is the Portuguese word for stone or boulder, but on Madeira the word is also used for beaches made up of such material. It’s a similar transference of meaning to that which gave the island its name. Madeira is Portuguese for wood (as in the material, rather than woodland), and the island was named for the dense laurisilva forest that almost completely covered it at the time of its discovery in the 15th century. Though now reduced to 20% of its former extent, it is still the largest surviving area of this subtropical forest and is protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

This calhau lies at the seaward terminus of the Ribeira de São Jorge. As you look inland, you can see the result of its work over the millennia — a deeply incised valley which cuts through many layers of volcanic history. Madeira is the summit of a massive shield volcano which began forming over 5 million years ago. As it has never been connected to the mainland, it is a paradise for plant lovers like me, with a remarkable number of endemic species, such as Helichrysum melaleucum and Matthiola maderensis.

These boulders may seem immovable, but the north of Madeira receives very high levels of rainfall, which can give the streams and rivers an awesome power to rework the land. The steep slopes are very susceptible to landslides and debris flows. I experienced this when I was there, having to avoid debris in the road after heavy winds and rain. Also, I was unable to get to one of the places I planned on visiting, since part of a major road has been closed for over two years.

Once material eroded from the valley reaches the coast, it is further reworked by, if anything, an even mightier force: the Atlantic. During substantial storms, the appearance of the beach and river mouth can change quite dramatically, assailed from both ends by a power surpassed, perhaps, by only one other in the history of this archipelago — the volcanic eruptions to which it owes its existence.
